newsitem.title: USA: U.S. official calls drug report "traumatic ritual".
newsitem.headline: U.S. official calls drug report "traumatic ritual".

text.p: The annual U.S. assessment of countries for their cooperation in fighting drug trafficking has become an "unnecessarily traumatic ritual," a senior State Department official said on Monday.

But Jeffrey Davidow, assistant secretary of state for inter-American affairs, warned a Washington conference that any attempt to change it could result in the U.S. Congress making the requirement even tougher.

At the demand of Congress, the State Department every year assesses, and "certifies" or "decertifies", 32 countries, many of them in Latin America, on whether they are helping U.S. anti-drug efforts. Aid can be suspended to countries that fail the test.

The process is causing increasing resentment abroad. When this year's decisions were announced Feb. 28, both Colombia, which was decertified for the second straight year, and Mexico, which was certified after much soul-searching in Washington, sharply criticised the exercise.
"I agree it has become, I think, an unnecessarily traumatic yearly ritual," Davidow told the Council of the Americas, a regional business forum, in reply to a question.
But, he said, "if we seek changes to the law...there is as much of an opportunity and chance that the law will be made more stringent as it will be made more comprehensive and understanding."

Davidow noted there was already an amendment circulating in Congress that would bar the administration from applying a national interests waiver that allows it to go on giving aid to some decertified countries.

"The view on the Hill (in Congress) is that if given an opportunity, those people down in the State Department would go soft...so we've really got to certify the State Department as much as we're certifying other countries," he added, to laughter.

Earlier, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said in an opening address to the conference that "the corrosive and corrupting effect of drug money hangs over much of the hemisphere like a mushroom cloud."

But Albright and other government speakers said the adoption of democratic systems and moves towards free-market economies in Latin America in recent years had greatly improved chances for economic progress in the region.

They also pointed to an increasing U.S. focus on the Americas, with President Bill Clinton making three trips there in the next year -- to Mexico, Costa Rica and Barbados next week, to South America in the fall, and to a regional summit in Santiago, Chile, next March.
Presidential counsellor Mack McLarty suggested that 1997 could be "the year of the Americas".

The Western hemisphere countries in 1994 set a target of expanding the existing North American Free Trade Agreement -- embracing the United States, Canada and Mexico -- into a Free Trade Area of the Americas by 2005.
Regional trade ministers meet next month in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, to consider moving towards negotiations on the issue.
"We must be ready, it seems to me, by the Santiago summit to launch these negotiations," Davidow said.
